Pregnancy

TORCH infections: pregnancy, newborn tests and follow-up

Updated: November 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

TORCH is a reminder of several infections that can affect a baby during pregnancy or around birth. It is not one disease, and there is no single treatment for a “TORCH infection”. The useful next step is to identify the organism, when exposure or infection occurred, and whether the baby needs assessment. An exposure or positive blood result does not by itself predict a child’s outcome.

What the letters mean, and what they leave open

The traditional letters refer to toxoplasmosis, “other” infections, rubella, cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex. The “other” group varies between services and may include syphilis, parvovirus B19, varicella and HIV. This is a clinical memory aid rather than a complete list of every infection relevant to pregnancy. Toxoplasma is a parasite and syphilis is bacterial; they are not all viruses.

Routes and timing differ. Some infections can cross the placenta, while others are particularly important during delivery or after birth. Effects can range from no apparent illness to problems with growth, the eyes, hearing, blood or nervous system. The name TORCH cannot tell you which problem is present, whether infection has reached the baby, or how severe it will be.

Testing should answer a specific clinical question

Routine antenatal infection screening is different from investigating a suspected congenital infection. An exposure, maternal illness, ultrasound finding or newborn examination may lead to particular tests. Laboratories do not all use “TORCH screen” to mean the same bundle. Ask which infection is being investigated, whose sample is needed and how the result will change care.

Antibody labels need interpretation. For example, CMV IgG can reflect an older infection, while CMV IgM alone cannot establish a recent primary infection. Additional testing and the history may be needed. A maternal result does not prove fetal damage. Newborn CMV requires a test for the virus, rather than an IgG/IgM panel. The correct sample and timing are as important as the test name.

Toxoplasmosis: a parasite with possible later eye problems

A new Toxoplasma infection during or shortly before pregnancy can pass to the developing baby. Many infected adults have no symptoms. Congenital infection can affect the brain and eyes, including seizures, head-size changes and vision problems. A baby may look well at birth and develop difficulties later, so appropriate follow-up matters even when there is no obvious early illness.

Prevention includes thoroughly cooking meat, washing produce and hands, and avoiding contamination from soil or cat faeces. You do not need to abandon a pet. Treatment during pregnancy is selected according to gestational timing and evidence of fetal infection; affected babies may need prolonged specialist treatment. Do not choose an antibiotic yourself or assume treatment can reverse every established injury.

Rubella: timing and protection before pregnancy matter

Rubella acquired in pregnancy can cause pregnancy loss or congenital rubella syndrome, with the greatest concern early in pregnancy. Possible effects include hearing loss, cataracts and heart defects, alongside other developmental or organ problems. A mild illness in the pregnant person does not show that fetal risk is small. Contact maternity care immediately after suspected infection or a relevant exposure.

There is no treatment that cures congenital rubella syndrome, but individual problems can be treated or supported. Vaccination before pregnancy is the main preventive step. MMR is not given during pregnancy; if protection is missing, discuss vaccination after birth. When vaccination is given before conception, follow the advised waiting interval, generally four weeks, rather than receiving it during pregnancy after an exposure.

CMV: hearing follow-up can matter after a normal newborn screen

CMV spreads through body fluids, including young children’s saliva and urine. Once acquired, it remains in the body and can reactivate; infection with another strain is also possible. Congenital CMV can therefore occur after a first infection or a later infection during pregnancy. Most affected babies do not develop health problems, while some have growth, brain, eye or hearing difficulties.

Hearing loss can develop later even after a passed newborn hearing screen. Suspected congenital CMV needs timely urine or saliva testing within the first three weeks; a positive saliva result is usually confirmed with urine. Ask promptly about testing rather than waiting for symptoms. Specialists assess whether antiviral treatment is appropriate, including for some babies with isolated hearing loss, and arrange hearing, vision and developmental follow-up.

Syphilis: timely treatment can prevent serious harm

Syphilis can pass to the baby during pregnancy even when the pregnant person has no obvious symptoms. Untreated infection can cause loss, prematurity or congenital disease affecting bones, blood, the liver, eyes or nervous system. Some newborns initially appear well. A fixed percentage from an old summary cannot predict an individual baby’s risk; the stage, treatment and timing matter.

Attend antenatal screening and any repeat tests advised by your maternity service. A positive result requires prompt assessment and appropriate penicillin treatment; an allergy needs specialist management rather than an unsupervised substitute. Partner assessment and follow-up help prevent reinfection. Babies exposed during pregnancy may need tests and treatment of their own, even after maternal treatment, depending on the clinical findings and treatment history.

Parvovirus B19: the main fetal concern is severe anaemia

Parvovirus B19 causes fifth disease, sometimes called slapped-cheek illness. Adults may have a new rash or joint pain, and many already have immunity. Exposure does not always produce infection, and infection does not usually harm the pregnancy. However, infection in the first half of pregnancy can sometimes cause severe fetal anaemia and pregnancy loss.

Contact your maternity team after a relevant exposure or symptoms. Blood tests can help assess immunity or infection, and additional ultrasound monitoring may be recommended if infection is confirmed. Specialist procedures are considered in selected affected pregnancies. Do not wait for the baby to seem less active or assume a mild maternal illness rules out the need for follow-up.

Chickenpox: congenital effects and newborn illness are different risks

Varicella-zoster virus causes chickenpox. Infection in early pregnancy carries a small risk of congenital varicella syndrome, which can involve skin scarring, limb differences and eye or brain problems. The often-quoted figure of up to about 2% refers to this syndrome after infection in early pregnancy, not the chance that the virus can pass to the baby at any time.

Chickenpox can also cause serious maternal illness, particularly pneumonia. Infection close to delivery creates a separate risk of severe newborn chickenpox. Contact the maternity service promptly after exposure or a new chickenpox-like rash; preventive treatment or antiviral care may be time-sensitive. The live varicella vaccine is not given during pregnancy. Immunity and vaccination plans are best reviewed before pregnancy or after birth.

HIV: early treatment and a planned infant testing schedule

HIV can pass during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding. Effective antiretroviral treatment, monitoring of viral load and appropriate newborn medicines greatly reduce transmission. Birth and feeding plans need specialist advice that considers the treatment response and local services. Having HIV does not automatically mean a baby will acquire it or that caesarean birth is always necessary.

An exposed infant needs an early testing plan, not a wait until symptoms appear or six months have passed. Tests that detect the virus are used because ordinary antibody tests can reflect antibodies passed from the parent. Repeat tests are needed at scheduled ages, with additional testing depending on medicines and feeding. Keep appointments and obtain help with medicine access or dosing questions promptly.

Herpes simplex: delivery and contact after birth both matter

Both HSV-1 and HSV-2 can cause genital infection. Transmission before birth is uncommon; exposure during delivery is especially important when genital herpes is first acquired near the birth. Tell your maternity team about previous herpes and any new genital sores, pain or burning. Antiviral treatment and birth planning depend on when infection began, symptoms and examination findings.

Caesarean birth may be advised for particular genital herpes circumstances; simply having a virus active somewhere in the body is not the rule. After birth, cold sores and other herpes lesions can also transmit infection. Do not kiss a baby when you have a cold sore, and wash hands before care. A baby with suspected neonatal herpes needs urgent specialist assessment and antiviral treatment.

A clear follow-up plan is more useful than a single label

Ask what has been confirmed, what remains uncertain, who will explain outstanding results and which checks are needed after birth. Depending on the infection, follow-up may involve hearing, vision, growth or developmental assessment. An infection diagnosis does not determine every future ability. Early support can address identified needs, while some babies remain well and need monitoring rather than treatment.

Seek prompt maternity advice for a concerning exposure, new rash or genital sores. A newborn who feeds poorly, has a fever of 38°C or higher, or develops sores needs urgent medical assessment. Use emergency services if a baby is difficult to wake, floppy, breathing abnormally, having a seizure or turning blue. Serious infection may occur without a rash; do not wait for a TORCH result before seeking help.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Testing and treatment are specific to the organism, pregnancy stage and newborn findings.

Routine antenatal screening differs from targeted investigation; local testing pathways can vary.

Current specialist CMV guidance includes assessment of isolated hearing loss; treatment needs an individual benefit–risk decision.

How BeMama can help

BeMama explains congenital-infection terminology and questions for your team. It cannot interpret a TORCH panel, diagnose fetal infection or choose pregnancy or newborn treatment.

When to seek help

Contact maternity care promptly after a concerning exposure, rash or genital symptoms. An unwell newborn needs urgent assessment, and a baby who is hard to wake, floppy, breathing abnormally, having a seizure or turning blue needs emergency help. Serious infection may have no rash. Do not wait for planned tests or change prescribed medicines yourself.

Evidence notes updated: November 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • TORCH groups different infections; it is not one diagnosis or one cure.
  • The organism, route, timing and clinical findings determine assessment.
  • A positive maternal antibody result alone cannot predict fetal injury.
  • Some newborn tests are time-sensitive, and later hearing or vision checks may be needed.
  • Prompt care and the recommended treatment can change outcomes; do not wait for a typical rash.

Frequently asked questions

Can chickenpox during pregnancy harm a baby?

Yes, but the risks depend on timing. Congenital varicella syndrome after early infection is uncommon; infection around delivery can cause a different, serious newborn illness. Contact maternity care promptly after exposure or a new rash so the team can assess immunity and treatment options.

Why is rubella important during pregnancy?

Infection, especially early in pregnancy, can affect the baby’s hearing, eyes, heart and other development or cause pregnancy loss. Suspected exposure needs immediate advice. MMR protects before pregnancy but is not given during pregnancy.

Can maternal syphilis be treated to protect the baby?

Yes. Prompt, appropriate penicillin treatment is central to preventing congenital syphilis. The baby may still need assessment based on the maternal treatment history and findings. Do not delay care because there is no rash or substitute another antibiotic yourself.

Does toxoplasmosis always cause obvious problems at birth?

No. Some congenitally infected babies initially look well, while eye or other problems can emerge later. Specialist treatment and follow-up depend on the diagnosis. A new maternal infection needs assessment rather than a prediction based on symptoms alone.

Should everyone request a TORCH blood panel?

The name does not define a universal screening package. Follow recommended antenatal screening and ask which specific infection needs investigation in your circumstances. Newborn tests may require urine, saliva or other samples rather than a standard antibody panel.

Does positive IgM mean my baby has been harmed?

No. Interpretation depends on the organism and the rest of the results. CMV IgM alone cannot establish a recent primary infection, and a maternal test does not diagnose fetal injury. Ask for a clinical explanation and any confirmatory tests.

Does herpes always require caesarean birth?

No. The timing of a first genital infection, current genital symptoms or signs, and the maternity team’s guidance matter. A history of a cold sore alone is not the same situation. Tell the team promptly about new symptoms, especially near delivery.

Can a baby who looks well still need follow-up?

Yes. Some congenital infections cause no signs at birth, and hearing or eye problems can appear later. Complete the agreed tests and follow-up. At the same time, a diagnosis does not mean that every possible complication will occur.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
